title: XX: The Minister in a Maze

teacherSummary.text: Walking home, Dimmesdale feels transformed and tempted to wicked acts: to argue blasphemy with a deacon, shock an old widow, corrupt a young maiden, teach children bad words and swear with a sailor. Mistress Hibbins hints that he has met the devil. He refuses Chillingworth's medicine, burns his sermon and writes a new Election Sermon all night.

satQuestions.passage: As the minister departed, in advance of Hester Prynne and little Pearl, he threw a backward glance; half expecting that he should discover only some faintly traced features or outline of the mother and the child, slowly fading into the twilight of the woods. So great a vicissitude in his life could not at once be received as real. But there was Hester, clad in her gray robe, still standing beside the tree-trunk, which some blast had overthrown a long antiquity ago, and which time had ever since been covering with moss, so that these two fated ones, with earth’s heaviest burden on them, might there sit down together, and find a single hour’s rest and solace. And there was Pearl, too, lightly dancing from the margin of the brook—now that the intrusive third person was gone—and taking her old place by her mother’s side. So the minister had not fallen asleep and dreamed!

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “No man, for any considerable period, can wear one face to himself, and another to the multitude, without finally getting bewildered as…” slowly and put it in my own words: The narrator says no one can show one face to himself and another to the crowd for long without becoming confused about which is true. Next, craft. I notice the general, proverb-like statement, which applies to Dimmesdale without naming him. The strongest word is “bewildered”: it means confused and lost, the state of a man who has lived a lie too long. Then, effect. What warning does the narrator give about double lives? My answer: The narrator warns that no one can wear one face to himself and another to the crowd without losing track of which is true; Dimmesdale's double life is destroying his sense of who he is.
